# Evidence

Proof that the end-to-end thread actually ran. This is a required deliverable (brief §6.3): the
saved capability artifact, a discovery log, and replay logs — including error paths.

**Everything here is regenerated by `make demo` and `make eval`.** Run ids are stable rather than timestamped, so a
reviewer can re-run the demo and diff the result against what is committed. Nothing here is
hand-written or edited after the fact.

---

## The runs

| Run | Terminal status | What it shows |
|---|---|---|
| [`discovery/demo-discovery/`](discovery/demo-discovery/) | — | The model driving the live UI to the goal. `run_record.json` names the model; `fake/scripted` means it ran from the recorded transcript because no API key was set. |
| [`replay/demo-success/`](replay/demo-success/) | `SUCCESS` | The same flow replayed with **different inputs** (`member_id=67890`) and **no model in the loop**. Three typed outputs. |
| [`replay/demo-business-outcome/`](replay/demo-business-outcome/) | `BUSINESS_OUTCOME` | `member_id=99999` → `member_not_found`, **exit code 0**. A legitimate answer, not a failure. |
| [`replay/demo-recovered-fault/`](replay/demo-recovered-fault/) | `SUCCESS` | An injected 502 matched the declared `transient_load` rule, the remedy cleared it, the run continued. `recovery_attempts=1`. |
| [`replay/demo-recovery-exhausted/`](replay/demo-recovery-exhausted/) | `NEEDS_HUMAN` | The same fault past its declared budget. Recovery is **bounded** — after 3 attempts it converts to `RECOVERY_EXHAUSTED` and escalates rather than retrying forever. |
| [`replay/demo-input-rejected/`](replay/demo-input-rejected/) | `FAILED` | A malformed argument rejected against the artifact's declared input pattern **before the browser moved**. Zero dispatches. |
| [`escalation/demo-escalation/`](escalation/demo-escalation/) | `NEEDS_HUMAN` | An undeclared screen → fail closed → a human takes the **live session** → acts → hands it back → the run re-anchors. |

| [`replay/demo-agent-found/`](replay/demo-agent-found/), [`demo-agent-missing/`](replay/demo-agent-missing/) | `SUCCESS`, `BUSINESS_OUTCOME` | A capability looked up **by name** from the catalog and invoked with typed arguments, as a production agent would. The second is a negative answer handled as an answer. |

All four terminal statuses are represented. The two most worth reading are the escalation and the
recovery-exhausted run.

## The measurements

`evidence/evals/` holds what `make eval` measured, rather than what the write-up asserts. Reports
only — the per-run traces behind them are working evidence and are gitignored.

| Report | What it answers |
|---|---|
| [`evals/replay_stability.md`](evals/replay_stability.md) | Does the same artifact keep working over many runs, and does it ever act on the wrong control? |
| [`evals/cross_tenant.md`](evals/cross_tenant.md) | Does it serve a **second institution** without being re-recorded? |
| `evals/*.evaluation.json` | The same data as a `CapabilityEvaluation` — derived data about a frozen capability, kept separate from it on purpose (ADR 0002). |

**The headline metric is wrong-action rate, and its target is zero.** A system that refuses is
acceptable: it escalates with full context. A system that clicks the wrong row in a core banking
screen is an incident. Refusal rate and wrong-action rate are reported separately and are never
traded off, because a system tuned to refuse less will eventually act on a control it was unsure of.

Wrong-action rate is measured against seeded ground truth in `apps/mock_bank/data.py`: a run counts
as wrong when it claims `SUCCESS` but any pinned output differs from that member's known value.
Against a real system this would have to come from a reconciliation source — the requirement is the
same, only the source of truth is harder.

Building the cross-tenant suite **falsified the reuse claim as it then stood**, which is the best
argument for having built it. See `REPORT.md` §7.

## Layout

```
capabilities/        the compiled draft and the reviewed capability, side by side
discovery/<run_id>/  the run that discovered the flow
replay/<run_id>/     deterministic replays: success, business outcome, and error paths
escalation/<run_id>/ a stuck run, a human takeover, and the resume
evals/               measured reports: stability and cross-tenant
evals-runs/          the traces behind those reports (gitignored: 16MB of working evidence)
```

`capabilities/` holding two artifacts is deliberate. `memberdesk.savings_balance` is what the
compiler produced from one discovery run — a **draft**, declaring no outcomes and no recovery rules,
with review notes saying exactly why. `corebank.member.savings_balance` is the **reviewed**
counterpart, declaring both. That pair is the `draft → approved` gate made visible, and
`cua catalog list` marks which is which.

Each run directory:

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `run_record.json` | The structured result: status, per-step actor / lease epoch / authorization / resolution strategy, drift, timings |
| `trace.jsonl` | Append-only event stream — `run_start`, `observe`, `resolve`, `authorize`, `dispatch`, `classify`, `recovery`, `lease`, `escalate`, `run_end` |
| `snapshots/` | The normalized `UiSnapshot` at each observation, redacted |
| `screenshots/` | Captured **on failure only** — a redacted PNG of what a human would have seen |

## How to read one

Start with `run_record.json`: it carries the terminal status and, on failure, the step, what was
expected and what was observed. `trace.jsonl` is the full story underneath.

**The record is a projection of the trace, not bookkeeping kept alongside it.** Every step's
`authorized` field is computed by matching its `dispatch` event to an `authorize` event with the
same `decision_id`, in the same file. So `unauthorized_dispatches` being empty is a statement about
what is on disk — not about what the executor believed it did. `tests/invariants/
test_policy_chokepoint.py` asserts the same correspondence against real evidence files.

Two things worth looking at specifically:

**The chokepoint, in the escalation run.** `run_record.json` shows automation acting at lease epoch
1, then the operator's two actions tagged `actor: human` at epoch 3, then lease transitions
`claimed → released → resumed`. Both human actions carry `authorized: true`. The operator went
through the same policy engine as the machine — that is the whole argument for the design, visible
as data.

**Failure capture.** The escalation trace's `note` event carries both a `snapshot_ref` and a
`screenshot_ref` for the moment things went wrong. Both are kept deliberately: the screenshot shows
what a human would have seen, the snapshot shows what the system actually perceived. A control that
is plainly visible in the image but absent from the tree is a perception bug, not a targeting bug,
and they are fixed in different places.

## On redaction

Every file here has passed through the `Redactor` — traces, snapshots, and screenshots alike, with
sensitive regions painted out of the images before they are written. The mock application is seeded
with fabricated data; no real credentials or personal information exist anywhere in this repository.

Over-redaction is a failure too. Capability references (`id@version`) once matched the email
pattern and were being masked, which made run records unable to say which capability had run.
`tests/invariants/test_redaction.py` now asserts both directions.
